tagline: What AI can't do for you, and how to grow your EQ

episodes.title: Meet Sena and Daniel: What AI Can't Do for You
episodes.short_title: What AI Can't Do for You
episodes.summary: Sena, an Associate in Tokyo, asks her mentor Daniel, a People Manager in Seattle, what is left for humans as AI gets better. Using research from Harvard Business School and BCG, the World Economic Forum, Gallup, Microsoft, and a meta-analysis on leaders' emotional intelligence, they set out the show's three human skills, judgment, trust, and growth, and the thread that runs through them all: EQ.
episodes.practice: Listen to someone without interrupting, then ask: "What do you think?"
sources: Dell'Acqua et al. (2023), Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, Harvard Business School Working Paper 24-013
World Economic Forum, Future of Jobs Report 2025
Gallup, research on managers and team engagement
Microsoft Work Trend Index 2025, The Year the Frontier Firm Is Born

Miao, Humphrey & Qian (2018), A cross-cultural meta-analysis of how leader emotional intelligence influences subordinate task performance and organizational citizenship behavior, Journal of World Business
Mattingly & Kraiger (2019), Can emotional intelligence be trained? A meta-analytical investigation, Human Resource Management Review

episodes.title: Interoceptive Awareness: The 30-Second Window
episodes.summary: A late-night message from a senior manager makes Sena's heart pound, and she almost sends a two-page apology. Daniel explains interoception, the sense that reads signals from inside your body, and why noticing them is the first EQ skill. They look at research on interoception and emotion, a study of traders on a London trading floor, and how naming a feeling can calm the brain's threat response. Then they turn it into a four-step habit: pause, scan, name, choose.
episodes.practice: Once a day, before replying to something that makes you react: pause, scan your body, name the feeling, then choose your next step. Write one sentence about it at night.
sources: Critchley & Garfinkel (2017), Interoception and emotion, Current Opinion in Psychology
Kandasamy et al. (2016), Interoceptive Ability Predicts Survival on a London Trading Floor, Scientific Reports
Lieberman et al. (2007), Putting Feelings Into Words: Affect Labeling Disrupts Amygdala Activity in Response to Affective Stimuli, Psychological Science
Gross (1998), Antecedent- and response-focused emotion regulation, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
